description: 85% hydration is very wet sourdough, close to ciabatta. Work out the water, starter, and salt for any flour weight, with the table and handling notes.

examples.result: Add 450 g flour, 375 g water, 100 g starter, and 10 g salt. Total dough 935 g.
steps: Starter is 20% of the flour: 500 × 0.20 = 100 g.
The starter is half flour and half water, so it brings 50 g of flour and 50 g of water.
Total water is 85% of the flour: 500 × 0.85 = 425 g. Water to add is 425 - 50 = 375 g.
Flour to add is 500 - 50 = 450 g. Salt is 2%: 500 × 0.02 = 10 g.

faqs.answer: High-protein bread flour, around 12.5% protein or more, is the safe choice. The Perfect Loaf's best sourdough recipe runs at 85% with medium-protein bread flour, and it works because the flour can absorb the water. All-purpose flour will struggle, and the dough will spread.
faqs.question: What flour works at 85% hydration?

faqs.answer: Because the starter already brings water. For 500 g of flour, 85% hydration means 425 g of water in total, and 100 g of starter brings 50 g of that water. You add the remaining 375 g. Adding all 425 g on top of the starter would push the true hydration to about 86%.
faqs.question: Why is the water to add only 375 g and not 425 g?

If the dough still has no strength after four sets of folds, your flour may not be able to take this much water, and 80% is the better target for that bag.

felicityNote: Eighty-five percent is a special-occasion dough in my kitchen, not a Tuesday dough. When it works, it is the best bread I make. When it does not, it is still excellent focaccia.

parts.meaning: Total flour in the dough, always 100% in baker's percentages. The starter's flour is part of it.
Total water as a share of total flour. At 85%, every 100 g of flour holds 85 g of water.
Starter as a share of total flour. At 20%, 500 g of flour takes 100 g of starter.
A 100% hydration starter is half flour and half water, so half its weight is flour and half is water.
Salt as a share of total flour. At 2%, 500 g of flour takes 10 g of salt.

formula.text: Starter = flour × starter %. Flour to add = flour - starter ÷ 2. Water to add = flour × hydration % - starter ÷ 2. Salt = flour × salt %.

howToSteps.name: Weigh the flour and water
howToSteps.text: Put the bowl on the scale, zero it, and weigh in the flour to add, then the water to add, holding back about 30 g of the water for now. The calculator already subtracted the starter's flour and water.

howToSteps.name: Add the starter and salt
howToSteps.text: Add the ripe starter, then the salt. Mix until no dry flour is left. The dough will be very wet and loose. Add the held-back water only if the dough feels like it can take it.

howToSteps.name: Rest, then fold
howToSteps.text: Cover the bowl and rest for 30 minutes. Then fold every 30 minutes for the first two to three hours: stretch and folds early, coil folds once the dough is full of air. Use wet hands throughout.

howToSteps.name: Bulk ferment and shape
howToSteps.text: Let the dough rise until it is about half as big again, domed, and jiggly. Shape with a bench scraper and wet hands, keeping the air in. A gentle envelope fold into the basket is enough.

howToSteps.name: Cold proof, then bake
howToSteps.text: Basket the loaf seam side up, cover, and refrigerate overnight. Bake straight from the fridge in a hot Dutch oven. If shaping defeats you, pour the dough into an oiled pan and bake focaccia instead.

lede: At 85% hydration the dough is very wet, close to ciabatta, and this is advanced sourdough: the biggest holes, the softest crumb, and the most demanding handling. Flour here means the total flour in the dough, including the flour inside the starter, so the hydration you ask for is the hydration you get.

name: 85% Hydration
summary: 500 g flour at 85% hydration: add 450 g flour, 375 g water, 100 g starter, 10 g salt.
title: Sourdough Calculator: 85% Hydration
tutorial: Eighty-five percent is the top end of sourdough hydration, and it is not a dough for a first bake. The Perfect Loaf's best sourdough recipe runs at 85%, and its author says plainly that it can be challenging and that beginners should hold water back. That is the right attitude: this hydration rewards experience, and it punishes a flour that cannot take the water.

The maths runs on baker's percentages, with flour always at 100%. For 500 g of total flour at 85% hydration, the dough holds 425 g of water in total. Your starter brings 50 g of that water, because 100 g of starter at 100% hydration is half flour and half water, so you add 375 g of water to the bowl. The starter also brings 50 g of flour, so you add 450 g of flour. Salt stays at 2%, which is 10 g.

The dough will look wrong when you mix it. It will be loose, sticky, and more like a batter than a dough, and the temptation is to add flour. Do not. The folds are what build the structure: stretch and folds early, coil folds once the dough is full of air, every 30 minutes for two to three hours. By the fourth set, a dough that looked hopeless will hold together, smooth out, and start to resist. If it never does, the flour is the problem, not you, and 80% is the right target for that bag.

High-protein bread flour is close to a requirement here. Around 12.5% protein or more gives the gluten network the strength to hold 85% water and still stand up in the oven. All-purpose flour absorbs less water, and an 85% dough made with it will spread no matter how well you fold it. Whole wheat and freshly milled flour absorb more, so they cope better, but they ferment faster, so keep an eye on the rise.

Shaping is the hardest part of an 85% loaf, and the honest fallback is to not shape it at all. Ciabatta and focaccia live in this hydration range precisely because they are baked flat or in a pan, so the dough never has to hold a tall shape. If the boule defeats you, pour the same dough into a well-oiled pan, dimple it, and bake focaccia. The crumb will be superb, and nobody at the table will know it was plan B.
